item.text:
`useEffect` synchronizes a component with something outside React: a subscription, timer, browser API, or network request. React runs it after a render commits. When dependencies change, React cleans up the old effect, then runs the new one. It also cleans up on unmount. [React reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffect)

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  const connection = connect(roomId);
  return () => connection.disconnect();
}, [roomId]);
```

Dependencies control when it runs:

- No array: after every commit.
- `[]`: on mount, with cleanup on unmount.
- `[roomId]`: on mount and when `roomId` changes.

**Common mistakes**

- Omitting a value used by the effect causes stale data. Include every reactive dependency; heed the linter.
- Updating a dependency on every run can cause a loop.
- Forgetting cleanup leaves subscriptions or timers active.
- Putting a new object or function in dependencies can trigger needless runs.
- Fetching without cancellation or an ignore guard can let an old response overwrite new data.
- Treating Strict ModeΓÇÖs extra development setup and cleanup cycle as a production bug hides missing cleanup. [React reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffect)

**Best practice:** Use an effect only to sync with an external system. Calculate display values during render; handle user actions in event handlers. Keep each effect focused, and make cleanup undo its setup. [React guide](https://react.dev/learn/you-might-not-need-an-effect)
